clue.text: He ensures stallholders keep to the right pitch and come in on time

definitions.text: He ensures stallholders keep to the right pitch and come in on time

parts.words: He ensures stallholders keep to the right pitch and come in on time
parts.note: the stallholders are singers sitting in church choir stalls, and pitch is musical pitch, not a market trader's patch

explanation.surface: A market superintendent keeps traders on their proper pitches and opening on time.
explanation.walkthrough: The market picture of stalls and pitches misleads: the stalls are those of a church choir, and the right pitch and coming in on time are singing matters.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who trains and conducts a church choir keeps the singers in tune and in time.

clue.text: Embarrassment of companion ends with a smile

indicators.note: the companion is followed at its end by the rest

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for Companion of Honour, a British order
a grin is a broad smile

explanation.surface: A friend's awkwardness finishes with a smile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'companion' is the crossword convention for the Companion of Honour, a British order; 'ends with' attaches the rest after it, and 'of' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Vexation from humiliation or disappointment is a near synonym for embarrassment.

clue.text: Part of a ship or dock

parts.note: to dock a tail is to cut or lop it

explanation.surface: A piece of a vessel or the harbour it sits in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dock' suggests a harbour, but it is the verb meaning to cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lowest deck of a sailing ship, so it is one part of the vessel.

clue.text: Adverse criticism of Boat Race — it's overridden

definitions.meaning: a scathing verdict on a rowing race, read as a dismal row
a track in Hyde Park, London, used for horse riding, so it is ridden over

explanation.surface: Critics savage the Boat Race, but their verdict is overruled.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition names a sandy riding track along the south side of Hyde Park in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The London bridleway is ridden over by horses daily, and a poor rowing contest might be scorned in those very words.

clue.text: Assent to a change of name

indicators.note: the letters of the word name are changed around

explanation.surface: Agreeing to switch to a new name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a change of' rearranges NAME; 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Said at the end of a prayer, the word expresses agreement, so it is an expression of assent.

clue.text: Visibly in tears

parts.note: tears here are rips in cloth, not weeping, so the phrase means plainly ripped

explanation.definitionFit: Clothing that is ragged and ripped is plainly in tears, the rending sense of the word.

clue.text: It's made to measure

parts.note: made to measure suggests tailoring, but means made for the purpose of measuring

explanation.definitionFit: A straight-edged strip marked in units exists for measuring length, so it is made to measure.

clue.text: Shakespearean character too involved about the underworld

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go around the underworld
the letters of too are tangled up into a new order

parts.note: hell is the underworld of the damned

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare role is overly concerned with the realm of the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'too involved' reads as overly concerned, but 'involved' scrambles the little word into OTO, and 'about' wraps that around the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moor of Venice is the title role of a Shakespeare tragedy.

clue.text: Scoundrel reconnoitred outside, took the plunge

indicators.note: the reconnoitring word goes outside the scoundrel

parts.note: to case a place is criminal slang for reconnoitring it
a cad is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A villain checked out a place before taking a risk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconnoitred' is criminal slang for checking out a target before a burglary; 'outside' says it goes round the scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that tumbled down in falls has literally plunged, as a waterfall does.

clue.text: A share in the plot

definitions.meaning: an apportioned portion given to someone
a small rented patch of ground for growing vegetables

explanation.surface: Someone owns a stake in a piece of land.
explanation.definitionFit: An apportionment is a share handed out, and a rented vegetable patch from the council goes by the same word.

clue.text: Lead a request for silence on the meadow

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another comes after it

parts.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
sh is the hushing sound asking for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone asks for quiet while walking out on a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a verb but is the dog's lead; 'on' in an across clue places the hush after the meadow, and 'the' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's lead and its strap or cord are synonyms for the same restraint.

clue.text: Badly criticised, having performed over the music

definitions.meaning: sharply rebuked, as when knuckles are struck
having delivered rhythmic spoken lyrics over a backing track, as in rap music

explanation.surface: A performer was savaged by critics after singing over the band.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sharply reprimanded is an idiom of striking, and performing rhyming lyrics over a beat is the hip-hop sense of the verb.

clue.text: Measured and mixed malt and rice

indicators.note: the letters of the two foodstuffs are stirred together into a new order

explanation.surface: A cook weighed out and combined malt and rice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' rearranges MALT and RICE together; 'and' joins the two words of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse that is measured has a regular rhythm, which is what poetic metre gives it.

clue.text: Motherly type?

parts.note: the figure of Mother ..., the personified natural world, rather than a caring woman

explanation.definitionFit: The natural world is personified as a mother figure, so it is a mother in that idiomatic sense.

clue.text: Teaching aid — supplying subjects for sermons?

definitions.meaning: a standard book used in a classroom
a book of scriptural passages, the texts preachers take as themes

explanation.surface: A classroom resource that also gives preachers their topics.
explanation.definitionFit: A school study book helps teaching, and a volume of passages that preachers take as texts is literally a book of texts.

clue.text: Andy's one to provide a non-committal answer

indicators.note: the letters of the name and the number are made to provide a new phrase by being rearranged

parts.note: the name with its S kept as a letter

explanation.surface: Andy is the one who always gives a vague reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to provide' signals rearranging ANDYS and ONE; the S of 'Andy's' counts as a letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying both affirmative and negative at once avoids committing to either side, an idiom for a hedged reply.

clue.text: A shop floor humiliation

parts.note: a department store basement is one of its floors

explanation.surface: A factory floor where workers are shamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shop floor' suggests factory workers, but it is a store's lowest level.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lowered in dignity or status is a synonym of humiliation.

clue.text: Dislike test said to be complicated

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made complicated, tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone says they hate an exam because it's too complex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be complicated' rearranges TEST SAID; 'said' is fodder, not a sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Aversion or distaste is a noun synonym for a dislike.

clue.text: One over the eight?

parts.note: one over the eight is slang for one drink too many, but here it is the person in charge of a rowing eight

explanation.definitionFit: The steersman of a racing boat directs its eight oarsmen, so is literally in command over them.

clue.text: I entered dream-home — in Spain suitably enough

indicators.note: the letter I enters, going inside, the home

parts.note: a castle in Spain or in the air is an idiom for a daydream home

explanation.surface: I walked into my ideal house in Spain, fittingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entered' puts I inside CASTLE. 'Castles in Spain' is an old idiom for daydreams, hence 'suitably enough'.
explanation.definitionFit: This historical kingdom is a region of central Spain, so it is found in Spain.

clue.text: Light vessel gets led astray

parts.note: a can is a container or vessel

indicators.note: the word led wanders off course, so its letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A ship's lamp leads a vessel the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astray' rearranges LED to make DLE; 'gets' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A wax stick with a wick is a source of light, so the noun light covers it.

clue.text: Novices losing head as breadwinners

indicators.note: the first letter of the novices is lost

parts.note: learners are novices, beginners at something

explanation.surface: Beginners who lose their way still bring home the money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' drops the L from LEARNERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who bring income into a household are the breadwinners, a synonym in the plural.

clue.text: Citizens taught in schools

definitions.meaning: people owing allegiance to a monarch or state
topics on the curriculum, such as history or maths

explanation.surface: Members of the public who learned things at school.
explanation.definitionFit: People under a sovereign's rule are her subjects, and the areas of study on a curriculum share the word.

clue.text: Relaxes when student leaves classroom equipment

indicators.note: the student departs, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: easels are stands for boards in a classroom
L is the learner plate abbreviation for a student

explanation.surface: Things get calmer when a pupil walks out of the classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes L out of EASELS; 'when' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease off is to relax, so the third-person verb forms match.

clue.text: Dive made by a footballer, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a ball struck with the head in football

explanation.surface: A footballer flings himself to the turf to win a free kick.
explanation.definitionFit: A headlong plunge is informally called this, and a football shot or pass with the head has the same name.

clue.text: Cut the cackle and use the tea cloth

definitions.meaning: stop talking, a slang order to be quiet

explanation.surface: Stop chattering and help with the washing-up.
explanation.walkthrough: A tea cloth is the British name for a tea towel used to wipe dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to fall silent and to wipe washed crockery after a meal.

clue.text: Beware of schoolboys

parts.note: a warning in old British public-school slang, from Latin meaning beware, shouted when a master approached

explanation.walkthrough: It is old British public-school slang, from Latin cavere, a lookout's warning that a teacher was coming.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin imperative served as a lookout's warning cry among British pupils of old.

clue.text: Though solid in form, they may have fragile footing

indicators.note: the letters of solid are put into a new form, or shape

explanation.surface: Statues may look solid yet stand on weak foundations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in form' signals rearranging SOLID; 'Though' only links. The definition alludes to 'feet of clay', a hidden flaw in someone admired.
explanation.definitionFit: Revered figures are proverbially said to have feet of clay, a flaw at the base of an admired image.

clue.text: Gluttons may have one, Alexander the Great didn't

definitions.text: Gluttons may have one, Alexander the Great didn't

parts.words: Gluttons may have one, Alexander the Great didn't
parts.note: a roll of belly fat round the waist, and also the Phoenician city Alexander besieged and sacked rather than leave unharmed

explanation.walkthrough: Alexander the Great destroyed the city of Tyre in 332 BC, so he did not leave it unharmed; the phrase also names a roll of fat round the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll of fat round the waist is idiomatically called an extra wheel cover, and the clue reads it again as a historical event.

clue.text: Sees pottery cast in moulds

indicators.note: the letters are cast, or thrown, into a new shape, as a potter would

explanation.surface: Someone watches clay pots being shaped in moulds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' rearranges SEES POTTERY; 'in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Printing plates cast from moulds gave the word its sense of a fixed, repeated pattern or template.
